# 03 · Joint, Conditional, Marginal — and Bayes {.unnumbered}

*The second concept in the spine, and the point at which probability starts being
useful. One new move — put **two** numbers on the same outcome instead of one —
produces the whole multivariate vocabulary: joints, marginals, conditionals, and
Bayes' rule. Everything here is elementary; the measure-theoretic version is
[in Perspectives](./11-joint-conditional-bayes.qmd) and is not needed.*

::: {.callout-note}
## Where this sits

Follows [Probability & Random Variables](./01-probability-101.qmd), which
introduced a single random variable on a sample space. Here two random variables
share an outcome, and that co-residence is the entire subject. The W02 primer
deck [Probability, Joints, Conditionals and Bayes](../materials/w02-deck-00-probability-joints.html){target="_blank"}
develops the same material from a 4 × 4 table of dice counts.
:::

## Two numbers on one outcome

Let $X$ and $Y$ be two random variables defined on the **same** sample space —
two numerical features read off the same outcome $\omega$. Height and weight of
one person; today's price and tomorrow's price of one stock; the clean image and
its noisy version from one generation run.

That sharing is the whole idea. "$X$ and $Y$ are jointly distributed" is not an
extra assumption bolted on; it is the statement that a single $\omega$ determines
both numbers at once, which is exactly why they can be correlated.

## Joint distributions

Let $X$ and $Y$ be two random variables defined on the same sample space — two
numerical features of the same outcome. Their **joint distribution** specifies
$p(x, y) = \mathbb{P}(X = x \text{ and } Y = y)$ in the discrete case, or a joint
density $f(x, y)$ whose volumes are probabilities in the continuous case. The joint
distribution is a complete description of the pair: every probabilistic statement
about $(X, Y)$ can be computed from it.

The following discrete joint distribution serves as the running example (the state
of a morning sky and the occurrence of rain):

| $p(x,y)$ | $Y{=}$ rain | $Y{=}$ no rain | row sum |
|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| $X{=}$ cloudy | 0.20 | 0.25 | **0.45** |
| $X{=}$ clear | 0.05 | 0.50 | **0.55** |
| column sum | **0.25** | **0.75** | 1 |

: {tbl-colwidths="[34,22,22,22]"}

## Marginal distributions

The **marginal** distribution of $X$ describes $X$ alone, with $Y$ disregarded. It
is obtained by summing (or, for densities, integrating) the joint distribution over
the other variable:

$$
p(x) = \sum_y p(x, y),
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
f(x) = \int f(x, y)\, dy .
$$

In the table these are the row and column sums — the margins of the table, which is
the origin of the term: $\mathbb{P}(\text{cloudy}) = 0.45$ and
$\mathbb{P}(\text{rain}) = 0.25$. The operation is justified directly by the
additivity axiom: the event "cloudy" is the disjoint union of "cloudy and rain" and
"cloudy and no rain". Marginalization recurs throughout the course; in the mixture
model of [Generative AI, in Its Simplest Form](./04-genai-simplest-form.qmd), the observed density
$p(x) = \sum_z p(z)\, p(x \mid z)$ is precisely the joint distribution of
$(x, z)$ with the latent variable summed out.

## Conditional distributions and Bayes' rule

The **conditional** distribution of $Y$ given $X = x$ is defined, whenever
$p(x) > 0$, by

$$
p(y \mid x) = \frac{p(x, y)}{p(x)} .
$$

The definition restricts attention to the outcomes consistent with $X = x$ and
renormalizes their probabilities to total 1. In the running example,
$\mathbb{P}(\text{rain} \mid \text{cloudy}) = 0.20 / 0.45 \approx 0.44$,
compared with the unconditional $\mathbb{P}(\text{rain}) = 0.25$.

Applying the definition in both directions and eliminating the joint yields
**Bayes' rule**,

$$
\boxed{\;p(x \mid y) = \frac{p(y \mid x)\, p(x)}{p(y)}\;}
$$

which converts a conditional in one direction into the conditional in the other.
The tanh denoiser of W01 is an application of this identity,
with $x$ the clean data point and $y$ the noisy observation; it is derived in full
in [The World's Smallest Diffusion Model](./05-two-point-diffusion.qmd).

$X$ and $Y$ are **independent** if $p(x, y) = p(x)\, p(y)$ for all $x, y$ —
equivalently, if $p(y \mid x) = p(y)$, so that conditioning on $X$ conveys no
information about $Y$. In the table, $0.20 \ne 0.45 \times 0.25$, so the two
variables are dependent. The i.i.d. assumption underlying the likelihoods of [Distributions and Maximum Likelihood](./02-distributions-mle.qmd)
are an independence statement applied to repeated observations.

## Bayes' rule, and why inference is the inverse problem

#### Generation runs forward; inference runs backward

Almost every model in this course is written in the **forward** direction. You
posit some unobserved state, and you write down a mechanism that turns it into
data:

$$
\underbrace{z}_{\text{latent, what we care about}}
\;\longrightarrow\;
\underbrace{x}_{\text{observed, what we get}} ,
\qquad \text{specified by } p(x \mid z).
$$

Writing $p(x \mid z)$ is usually the easy half. It is a *mechanism* — a
simulator, a physical story, a noise model — and you can often just state it.

But that is rarely what you want. You do not observe $z$; you observe $x$, and
you want to reason back to the cause. That is the **inverse problem**:

$$
\underbrace{x}_{\text{observed}} \;\longrightarrow\; \underbrace{z}_{\text{inferred}},
\qquad \text{wanted: } p(z \mid x).
$$

| | Forward | Inverse |
|---|---|---|
| Direction | cause $\to$ effect | effect $\to$ cause |
| Object | $p(x \mid z)$ | $p(z \mid x)$ |
| Typical status | given, by modelling | wanted, must be computed |
| Names | generative model, sampling distribution, simulator | inference, inversion, the posterior |

You cannot simply invert the arrow, because the forward map is generally
**many-to-one**: different latent states can produce the very same observation.
Knowing $x$ therefore does not determine $z$ — it only makes some values of $z$
more plausible than others. Something extra is needed to break the tie, and that
something is what you believed about $z$ before looking. Bayes' rule is exactly
the bookkeeping that combines the two:

$$
\underbrace{p(z \mid x)}_{\text{posterior}}
\;=\;
\frac{\overbrace{p(x \mid z)}^{\text{likelihood}}\;\overbrace{p(z)}^{\text{prior}}}
     {\underbrace{p(x)}_{\text{evidence}}},
\qquad
p(x) = \sum_z p(x \mid z)\,p(z).
$$

This is the single most useful thing in the course's toolkit: **it is the bridge
from the direction you can write down to the direction you want.**

#### A toy example: did the student understand "or"?

A student is set ten short questions on the logical connective **or**. We would
like to know whether they have actually grasped it — but "understanding" is not
something we can measure. We can only mark the answers.

- **Latent** $z \in \{0, 1\}$: the student understands the concept, or does not.
  This is the *inferential goal*.
- **Observable** $x \in \{0, 1, \dots, 10\}$: the number of questions correct.
  This is all we ever see.

Now the forward model — the **sampling distribution** that says how marks are
produced given the latent state. A student who understands still slips
occasionally; one who does not can still get items right by guessing or by luck
in which items came up. Take each item as independent with

$$
x \mid z = 1 \;\sim\; \text{Binomial}(10,\ 0.9),
\qquad
x \mid z = 0 \;\sim\; \text{Binomial}(10,\ 0.4).
$$

::: {.callout-note}
## The marks scale does not matter

Nothing above depends on marks running $0$ to $10$. The same structure works for
a single right/wrong item ($x \in \{0,1\}$, a Bernoulli), or a percentage score
$0$–$100$, or a graded rubric. All that changes is the count distribution you
put on the observable. What stays fixed is the shape of the problem: a latent
you want, an observable you get, and a sampling distribution connecting them.
:::

Suppose the student scores $x = 7$. Take a neutral prior $p(z=1) = 0.5$. Then

$$
\frac{p(z=1 \mid x=7)}{p(z=0 \mid x=7)}
= \underbrace{\frac{\binom{10}{7} 0.9^{7} 0.1^{3}}{\binom{10}{7} 0.4^{7} 0.6^{3}}}_{\text{likelihood ratio}}
\times \underbrace{\frac{0.5}{0.5}}_{\text{prior odds}}
= \Big(\tfrac{0.9}{0.4}\Big)^{7}\Big(\tfrac{0.1}{0.6}\Big)^{3}
= 1.352 ,
$$

so $p(z = 1 \mid x = 7) = 1.352 / 2.352 = \mathbf{0.575}$.

Two things are worth noticing. The binomial coefficient $\binom{10}{7}$ appears
in both the numerator and the denominator and **cancels** — it describes how many
ways the marks could have been arranged, which is the same under either
hypothesis, so it carries no evidence. And $7/10$, which sounds like a decent
score, is barely informative here: it moves us from $50\%$ to $58\%$.

Across the range of possible scores:

| Score $x$ | 3 | 5 | 7 | 9 | 10 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $p(z = 1 \mid x)$ | 0.000 | 0.007 | 0.575 | 0.996 | 1.000 |

The posterior is not a smooth reflection of the mark — it is nearly flat at the
extremes and swings sharply in the middle, where the two hypotheses actually
disagree.

And the prior genuinely matters. At the same score $x = 7$:

| Prior $p(z=1)$ | 0.2 | 0.5 | 0.8 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Posterior $p(z=1 \mid x=7)$ | 0.253 | 0.575 | 0.844 |

Same evidence, three different conclusions. This is not a defect. It is the
honest statement that seven out of ten is weak evidence, and weak evidence does
not overturn what you already knew.

#### The sampling distribution *is* the likelihood

The expression $p(x \mid z)$ has been doing two jobs above, and it is worth
separating them, because this is the distinction
[Distributions and Maximum Likelihood](./02-distributions-mle.qmd)
makes in the parametric setting.

| Hold fixed | Vary | You get | Sums to 1? |
|---|---|---|---|
| the latent $z$ | the data $x$ | the **sampling distribution** — how marks come out | yes, over $x$ |
| the observed data $x$ | the latent $z$ | the **likelihood** — how well each $z$ explains what we saw | no |

It is one formula read in two directions. Forward, it generates. Backward, it
scores. Bayes' rule is what converts the backward reading into an actual
probability distribution over $z$, by weighting with the prior and renormalising.

#### Bayesian Knowledge Tracing

The toy example freezes the student in time. Real learners *learn*, so the latent
state changes as they work — and the natural extension is exactly the model used
in intelligent tutoring systems: **Bayesian Knowledge Tracing** (Corbett and
Anderson, 1995, *User Modeling and User-Adapted Interaction*).

BKT keeps the same two-layer structure and lets the latent evolve:

- a hidden binary skill state $z_t \in \{\text{not known}, \text{known}\}$;
- an observed response $x_t \in \{\text{incorrect}, \text{correct}\}$ at each
  opportunity $t$.

Four parameters specify it, and each is a conditional probability:

| Parameter | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $P(L_0)$ | probability the skill is known before any practice — the **prior** |
| $P(T)$ | probability of learning it at an opportunity, if not yet known — the **transition** |
| $P(G)$ | probability of answering correctly *without* knowing it — the **guess** |
| $P(S)$ | probability of answering incorrectly *while* knowing it — the **slip** |

So the emission model is $P(\text{correct} \mid \text{known}) = 1 - P(S)$ and
$P(\text{correct} \mid \text{not known}) = P(G)$. Standard BKT assumes no
forgetting.

Tracing a student is then a two-step recursion, repeated per question — and the
first step is precisely Bayes' rule:

1. **Update on the evidence.** With $L$ the current probability the skill is
   known, a correct answer gives
   $$
   L^{+} \;=\; \frac{L\,(1 - P(S))}{L\,(1 - P(S)) + (1-L)\,P(G)} ,
   $$
   and an incorrect answer gives
   $L^{-} = L\,P(S) \,/\, [\,L\,P(S) + (1-L)(1 - P(G))\,]$.
2. **Predict forward through learning.** $L \leftarrow L^{\pm} + (1 - L^{\pm})\,P(T)$.

For instance with $L = 0.4$, $P(S) = 0.10$, $P(G) = 0.25$, $P(T) = 0.20$, a
correct answer raises the belief to
$0.36 / 0.51 = 0.706$, and the learning step then carries it to
$0.706 + 0.294 \times 0.20 = 0.765$ before the next question. An incorrect answer
instead drops it to $0.04/0.49 = 0.082$.

::: {.callout-tip}
## The shape to remember

A latent state you care about, an observable you actually get, a forward model
connecting them, and Bayes running the inference backwards — repeated over a
sequence. That is BKT, and it is also a hidden Markov model, a Kalman filter,
and, as the next few weeks will show, a diffusion model.
:::

#### Why this is the shape of the whole course

Diffusion models are an inverse problem, and it is worth being blunt about the
terminology, because it inverts what you might expect.

- The **forward process** of a diffusion model is the *corruption*:
  $x_0 \to x_\sigma = x_0 + \sigma z$. We write it down ourselves, in closed
  form, and it is trivial to sample. This is the easy direction.
- **Generating an image** means going the other way — recovering a plausible
  clean $x_0$ from a noisy $x_\sigma$. The clean signal is the latent; the noisy
  observation is the data.

So in a diffusion model, *generation is the inference problem*. That is why the
central object of the course is a posterior, and why the optimal denoiser is a
posterior **mean**:

$$
\mathbb{E}[x_0 \mid x_\sigma]
= \tanh\!\Big(\frac{x_\sigma}{\sigma^2}\Big)
\quad\text{for the two-point dataset of }
$$
W01 — which, as
[Joint, Marginal, Conditional](./11-joint-conditional-bayes.qmd) shows,
is nothing but Bayes' rule applied to two Gaussian shelves and then averaged.
Swap "understands the concept" for "was a $+1$", and "ten marks" for "one noisy
measurement", and it is the same calculation you did above.

## Exercises

1. Two fair coin tosses. Let $X$ be the result of the first toss and $Y$ the
   total number of heads. Write the joint as a table, compute both marginals, and
   compute both families of conditionals. Verify Bayes' rule on
   $\mathbb{P}(X = H \mid Y = 1)$.
2. For the sky-and-rain table above, compute
   $\mathbb{P}(\text{cloudy} \mid \text{rain})$ by Bayes' rule from
   $\mathbb{P}(\text{rain} \mid \text{cloudy})$ and the marginals, then confirm it
   by reading the table directly.
3. Construct two *different* joint distributions on $\{0,1\}^2$ that have the same
   pair of marginals. What does this show about whether marginals determine a
   joint?
4. Show that if $p(x,y) = p(x)p(y)$ then every conditional $p(y \mid x)$ equals
   $p(y)$ — independence means the conditional does not move as you change what
   you condition on.
5. In the mixture model $z \sim \text{Bernoulli}(\pi)$,
   $x \mid z \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_z, \sigma^2)$: identify the joint $p(x,z)$, both
   marginals, and both conditionals. State which of these the
   [W01 denoiser](./05-two-point-diffusion.qmd) computes, and which the ancestral
   sampler of
   [Generative AI, in Its Simplest Form](./04-genai-simplest-form.qmd) uses.
6. A generative model produces a noisy observation $x_t$ from a clean signal
   $x_0$. Which direction is easy to write down, $p(x_t \mid x_0)$ or
   $p(x_0 \mid x_t)$? Which one does generation require? Name the rule that
   converts one into the other.
